doc.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: Early life and the Air Force
title: Drafted into the segregated Air Force band in Greensboro
summary: He is drafted, sends for his horn, and joins a Negro band at Greensboro, where racism affected life off base.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: said no I like that better than the others. Then I heard Coleman Hawkins, and Prez. Now when I heard Hawk, he didn’t knock me out like Lester Young did. But when I got older, I realized that Hawk was playing the changes better than Lester Young. But Lester Young had that beat and that sound, you know [scats]. Oh I like that boy. And then when I heard Charlie Parker and Dizzy, I said that settles that. That’s it. Yep. So that’s how that happened. And then I was drafted in the Air Force. And they said, “Does anyone here play an instrument?” No — they said, “Do you have an instrument?” And I said, “Yeah, I’ve got one.” They said, “Send for it.” They didn’t ask if you could play it, they said if you had it. I said yeah. So I sent for the instrument and they formed a band. And in those days, like it was segregated, and I was stationed in Greensboro, North Carolina. So they had a segregated — like they wanted to have — the base was like, say this is the base like this. This one quarter here was Negro and the other three-quarters was Caucasian, all right? So they wanted a Negro band. So that’s what they did, they formed one. And they had the official Air Force Band come over and teach the Negro band. They taught us. And then in about a year or so, man, our band was really nice, it sounded good. So they would come over and listen to our band. And I made some good friends with some of the guys because like even now when I play, one of the clarinet players, he always comes by if he’s in town for the gig when I play it. Says, “Hey Moody, remember” so-and-so? Yeah I remember man. I was eighteen years old.
Did your band ever go to play for the white servicemen?

Oh yeah. You played for the officers, oh yeah, you played for them you know, like that. We were down there, I was stationed in Greensboro, and I’m not sure if the Tuskegee Airmen came by there or not, but I remember there was trouble in town one night and it had to do with officers. Because as I was telling about the German prisoners of war jumping off the trucks and going in the restaurants eating in Greensboro, and I couldn’t go and eat in the restaurants because I was a Negro you see? So there was some kind of problem in town. And I was wondering if that could have had something to do with the Tuskegee Airmen who were there, because this was an overseas replacement. Before, when I went there, it was BTC # 10. Basic Training Center #10. Then it changed over to ORD. Replacement Depot. Overseas Replacement Depot. And I’m wondering if the Tuskegee Airmen were getting ready to go overseas and that’s when they had some of the problems in town, because the racism was rampant.
